opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting questions in biology right now. The way drug discovery works today is fundamentally a process of trial and error. You come up with a hypothesis about a target, you screen enormous libraries, and you push candidates through a long funnel where something like ninety percent of what enters clinical trials fails. Most of those failures aren't because people weren't smart. They're because biology is incredibly complex and we just don't have good ways of predicting what will happen when you perturb a living system.

So the promise of predictive models is to move more of that trial and error from the wet lab into the computer. You can think about it at a few levels. At the molecular level, models are getting very good at predicting structure, binding, and increasingly function: designing proteins, antibodies, and small molecules with specific properties instead of finding them by brute-force screening. That's already happening, and it's compressing timelines for the early discovery stages.

But I think the bigger opportunity, and honestly the harder one, is at the cellular and systems level. Most drugs don't fail because they don't bind their target. They fail because the target was wrong, or because hitting it causes effects you didn't anticipate. What we really want are models that can simulate how a cell responds to a perturbation, what we sometimes call a virtual cell. If you could ask, "If I knock down this gene or add this compound in this cell type, from this patient, what happens to the cell's state?" and get a reasonably accurate answer, that changes everything about how you pick targets and design trials.

We're not there yet. The data is a real bottleneck. Biology hasn't had its internet-scale dataset in the way language did, so a lot of the work is generating perturbation data at scale specifically to train these models, and building the right benchmarks so we know whether they're actually learning biology or just memorizing patterns.

If it works, I think the practical effect is that you go from an industry where you test maybe a handful of hypotheses very expensively to one where you can explore huge spaces of hypotheses computationally and then only take the most promising ones into the lab. It doesn't eliminate experiments, but it makes each experiment far more informative. That's how you bend the cost curve and the success rate, which ultimately means more medicines reaching patients faster.

r001.rationale: The response describes drug discovery as trial and error with a long validation funnel, and says researchers lack good ways to predict biological outcomes.

r002.rationale: It says predictive models could simulate cellular responses and let researchers computationally explore huge spaces of hypotheses before selecting candidates for lab experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the models themselves are not really the bottleneck. The bottleneck is the data we feed them, and that is where I think the biggest shift is going to happen.

If you look at how drug discovery works today, it is fundamentally an empirical, trial-and-error process. You have a hypothesis about a target, you screen a huge library of molecules against it, you get a hit, you spend years optimizing it, and then you go into animals and eventually people, and most of the time it fails. Roughly ninety percent of programs that enter clinical trials do not make it. And they usually fail for reasons that have nothing to do with chemistry. They fail because the biology was wrong. The target did not matter in humans the way it mattered in a mouse or a dish.

So the question I get excited about is: can a predictive model actually learn biology well enough to tell you, before you spend a decade and a billion dollars, that this is the right target in the right patient population? To do that you need something that looks less like a chemistry model and more like a virtual cell. A model that has seen enough perturbations, enough genetic knockouts, enough drug treatments across enough cell types, that it can simulate what happens when you push on a given node in the system.

The reason I think we are close is that for the first time we can generate that kind of data at scale on purpose. With CRISPR and single-cell readouts, you can knock out every gene in the genome, in hundreds of thousands of cells, and read out the full transcriptional consequence of each one. That is a training set that was simply not available five years ago. Instead of scraping whatever experiments happened to be published, you can design the experiment to teach the model what you want it to know, and then close the loop: the model proposes the next set of perturbations, you run them, and it gets better.

If that works, the discovery process stops being a funnel where you throw away ninety-nine point nine percent of what you make, and starts looking more like engineering. You design the intervention, you predict the effect, and you go to the lab mainly to verify rather than to search. I do not think it collapses the timeline to zero, because you still have to run the trial in people. But I think it could flip the failure rate, and that alone would transform the economics of medicine.

r001.rationale: It describes discovery as trial and error, with sequential screening and clinical testing, and says models could predict the right target and patient population before those costly steps.

r002.rationale: It says a virtual-cell model could simulate perturbation effects and guide experiments, but does not communicate that drug-discovery experiments would be simulated in parallel.

astra-6.text:
I think the big opportunity is to make drug discovery much more predictive and much less dependent on trial and error. Today, you can find something that looks promising in a simplified experimental system, spend years developing it, and then discover that it doesn’t work in people. A lot of that comes down to how little we can predict about biology across those different contexts.

Imagine being able to ask: If I perturb this gene or give this molecule to a particular cell, what happens? And how does that response change depending on the patient’s genetic background or the state of their disease? If models can answer those questions reliably, they could help us choose better targets, design better molecules, and identify which patients are most likely to benefit.

The key is connecting prediction to experiment. You want a model that helps you choose the most informative experiments, then learns from the results—including the failures. That could turn drug discovery into a much faster learning cycle. You’d still need experimental and clinical validation, but you could make much better decisions about what to take forward.

r001.rationale: It describes discovery as relying on trial and error and says limited ability to predict biology across experimental and human contexts leads to years of development before failures emerge.

r002.rationale: It discusses using models to predict biological responses and choose informative experiments, but does not identify running or simulating drug-discovery experiments in parallel.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big opportunity is to make drug discovery much more predictive and less dependent on trial and error. Today, you can identify a promising target, find a molecule that affects it, and still have very little confidence about what will happen when you put that molecule into a person. Does it reach the right tissue? Does it have unexpected effects? Will it actually change the course of disease?

If we can build models that predict how biological systems respond to an intervention, we can explore many more possibilities computationally and use experiments to test the most informative ones. Then those experimental results improve the model. That feedback loop could help us choose better targets and design better therapies earlier in the process.

The crucial thing is that predicting a pattern isn’t the same as predicting what happens when you change something. For drug discovery, you need models that can handle interventions and make useful predictions beyond the data they were trained on. Ultimately, the test is whether they help us develop medicines that work in patients.

r001.rationale: It describes low confidence about a molecule’s effects in people and says models could reduce trial and error, but does not explain that drug discovery relies on sequential empirical validation because predictive power is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It says models could explore many more possibilities computationally while experiments test the most informative ones, conveying parallel computational exploration of drug-discovery possibilities.
